did_you_know.text: The Torah calls the document a “sefer keritut,” while the Sages call it a “get.” The word “keritut” is connected with the idea of cutting off and ending the relationship.
The two millstones were a lower stone and an upper stone. Without either one, grain could not be ground, so taking one away threatened a family’s ability to obtain food.

The verse stresses that kidnapping and selling a person is not ordinary theft, but a serious attack on human freedom. In the ancient world, where slavery was common, the Torah especially condemns selling a fellow Israelite into slavery.
Biblical “tzaraat” is not necessarily the disease known today as leprosy. It refers to various skin conditions examined by priests, mainly to determine a person’s ritual status.
A garment taken as security could also serve as a blanket at night. Returning it before bedtime was therefore not merely an economic rule, but protection of a poor person’s basic needs.
Poor laborers in the ancient world often lived on that day’s wages rather than monthly savings. Delaying payment could leave their families without food.

During the grape harvest, a farmer was not to go over every vine repeatedly to collect every last grape. The Torah required leaving part of the crop for people without land, creating a dignified way to support them.
